chapters.working: Hyde Park, the Ground That Keeps Moving

narrationBeats: Open on camera, present day, standing in Hyde Park on the South Side of Chicago. A lakefront neighborhood roughly seven miles south of the Loop.
Set the hook plainly. The ground here looks settled. Old stone houses, a major university, a Frederick Law Olmsted park along the lake. It reads as permanent. It is not.
State the thesis without giving away the history. This is a place that has been built and rebuilt again and again. Powerful institutions kept reshaping the ground under the people who lived here.
Name the pattern that the rest of the tour will follow. A railroad, a world's fair, a university, a federal program. Each one redrew the map. Each one decided who stayed and who had to move.

Ground the claim in one concrete, verifiable fact for the cold open. In the 1950s urban renewal that the University of Chicago helped drive, more than fifteen thousand people were displaced as buildings were bought, condemned, and torn down. Hold that number. Do not explain it yet.
Foreshadow the present. The reshaping is not over. The Obama Presidential Center is under construction right now in Jackson Park, on Hyde Park's edge, the same parkland that held the 1893 fair.

Close the cold open by handing the audience the question the tour answers. Who keeps deciding what this neighborhood becomes, and what happens to the people already living on the ground when they decide.
facts: Hyde Park began in 1853 when real estate speculator Paul Cornell bought roughly 300 acres of lakefront land between 51st and 55th streets and named it after the London park.
Hyde Park Township stayed politically independent until it was annexed to the city of Chicago in 1889; central Hyde Park residents opposed annexation while areas farther south voted for it.
The University of Chicago was established in the neighborhood in 1890 with funding from John D. Rockefeller and leadership from William Rainey Harper.
The World's Columbian Exposition ran in Jackson Park and along the Midway Plaisance from May 1 to October 30, 1893, drew more than 27 million visitors, and was nicknamed the White City.
Hyde Park urban renewal cleared housing through the 1950s; work began in May 1955 and the City Council approved the plan on November 7, 1958. More than 15,000 residents were displaced.

After renewal, average income in Hyde Park rose about 70 percent while the Black population fell about 40 percent, since condemned substandard housing had largely been occupied by low-income Black residents.
The Barack Obama Presidential Center is under construction on a 19.3-acre campus in Jackson Park, on the border of Hyde Park and Woodlawn, the same parkland that held the 1893 fair.

verify.notes: Most of the researcher's material holds up, but one beat contained a hard factual error and several claims needed sharpening. CRITICAL FIX: the Obama Presidential Center is no longer under construction. It opened to the public on June 19, 2026 (Juneteenth), days before this publication date of June 23, 2026. Any present-tense 'under construction right now' language must be removed; the defensible framing is that it opened in June 2026. CONTESTED NUMBERS: (1) The 15,000-displaced figure is the one University of Chicago's own sources use and is safe with 'more than 15,000,' but Chicago Magazine cites 30,000 for the broader redevelopment area around campus, so do not present 15,000 as a hard ceiling. (2) The 27-million fair-attendance figure is the popular number but is soft. Britannica gives about 21.5 million paid admissions and about 25.8 million total; 27-28 million reflects double-counting. script.voiceover: On the South Side of Chicago, about seven miles from downtown, a neighborhood called Hyde Park runs right up to Lake Michigan. Its greystones and Gothic towers look permanent, as if they had always stood here. Almost none of it was here a hundred and seventy years ago. Since then, Hyde Park has been built, cleared, and rebuilt, again and again, by institutions with money and a plan. A railroad reached the prairie first. Then a university, then a World's Fair. In the 1950s, a federal urban renewal program pushed more than fifteen thousand people off their blocks. Most of them were never asked. This is the story of who keeps deciding what this neighborhood becomes, and what happens to the people already living here.

script.hostScript: I’m standing in Hyde Park, on the South Side, about seven miles south of downtown. Look at these greystones. They feel like they were here before anybody, and like they’ll outlast all of us. But this block looks the way it does because powerful institutions kept deciding it should, and plenty of people got moved so it could happen. This is some of the most reshaped ground in Chicago, and the people doing the reshaping had money and a plan, and almost none of them lived here. So here is the question I want us to carry the whole way through. Who keeps deciding what this neighborhood becomes, and what happens to the people already here when they do.

script.voiceover: Before any of this, the ground was prairie and marsh, sloping down to the lake. It was Potawatomi land, part of the Council of Three Fires, who had lived and traded along these shores for generations. They did not fight the Black Hawk War of 1832, but in its wake the United States pressed the Three Fires nations into the Treaty of Chicago, in 1833. With one signing they gave up some five million acres, this lakefront among them, and within a few years they were marched west. Around 1835 a settler named Nathan Watson raised a tavern near what is now 53rd Street and the water, on the old trail the Potawatomi had walked. The first taking set the pattern. This ground would be claimed, cleared, and remade, again and again, by whoever held the deed and the plan. In 1853 a young lawyer named Paul Cornell bought three hundred acres from Watson's widow.

narrationBeats: Paul Cornell was born August 5, 1822, and came to Chicago in 1847 to practice law. He was a real estate speculator and a cousin of Ezra Cornell, who founded Cornell University.

In 1853 Cornell bought 300 acres of lakefront land between 51st and 55th Streets along Lake Michigan, several miles south of the small city of Chicago. He named the tract Hyde Park after the London park.

The land only had value if people could reach it. Cornell deeded 60 acres to the Illinois Central Railroad. In exchange he secured a station at 53rd Street and a commitment of six daily trains each way to Chicago's Central Depot downtown.

The railroad deal turned a remote stretch of prairie and lakeshore into a commuter suburb and a resort. Cornell marketed Hyde Park to wealthy Chicagoans who wanted leisure and distance from the crowded city.
In 1857 Cornell built the Hyde Park House, a four-story wood-frame hotel on the lake near the 53rd Street station. It was the center of Hyde Park social life until it burned in an 1879 fire.

The hotel drew prominent guests. The Prince of Wales, Albert Edward, stayed during his 1860 visit to Chicago. Mary Todd Lincoln stayed there with her sons Robert and Tad for about two and a half months after Abraham Lincoln's assassination in 1865.
Within roughly ten years the settlement had about 1,000 residents. Cornell became known as the father of Hyde Park for buying and developing extensive land in the 1850s.

In 1861 the Illinois General Assembly created Hyde Park Township, a unit of local government much larger than the neighborhood itself. It ran from 39th Street on the north to 138th Street and the Calumet River on the south, and from State Street on the west to Lake Michigan and the Indiana state line on the east.
The township grew fast. Its population rose from 15,716 in 1880 to roughly 85,000 by 1889, a more than fivefold increase in less than a decade.

On June 29, 1889, Hyde Park Township voters approved annexation to the City of Chicago, along with several other suburban townships. Chicago offered better water, sewers, and fire and police protection. The vote folded a large part of the South Side into the city.

Cornell also pushed for the South Park system that produced Jackson Park and Washington Park, and he lived to see the University of Chicago founded in 1890 on land near his original tract. He died March 3, 1904, and is buried at Oak Woods Cemetery.

removedClaims: The Prince of Wales, Albert Edward, stayed at the Hyde Park House during his 1860 visit to Chicago. REASON: contested and not safely supportable. The well-documented 1860 royal visit places the official party at the Richmond House downtown (arrived September 21, 1860, three-day stay). Most sources frame the hotel's life as ending around 1879, but at least one source dates the destroying fire to September 1877, and the Wikipedia article gives '1857 until 1879' without explicitly stating a fire in that year. Softened to 'destroyed by fire near the end of the 1870s.'
The hotel being described as a 'resort' on the lake 'near the 53rd Street station' kept, but the precise claim that it 'burned in an 1879 fire' was changed to avoid asserting a contested year.

narrationBeats: The University of Chicago that stands in Hyde Park today is the second school to carry that name. An earlier University of Chicago, a Baptist college founded in 1856 on land donated by Senator Stephen A. Douglas, sat in what is now Bronzeville. It struggled with debt for decades and closed in 1886 after foreclosure. The new school was a separate legal entity with no financial tie to the first.

The campaign for a new Baptist university in Chicago ran through the American Baptist Education Society. Frederick T. Gates became the society's secretary in 1888 and pressed the cause. Thomas W. Goodspeed of the Morgan Park Theological Seminary worked alongside him. Both wanted a great Baptist university in Chicago and both lobbied John D. Rockefeller, the Standard Oil magnate, to fund it.

Rockefeller made his offer at the society's meeting in Boston on May 18, 1889. He pledged $600,000 toward an endowment, on the condition that another $400,000 be raised from other donors. The income from the endowment could cover expenses but not land or buildings. Gates and Goodspeed ran a two-man solicitation campaign through 1889 and 1890 and raised the matching $400,000.

The University of Chicago was incorporated on September 18, 1890. The university dates its founding to July 1, 1891. Rockefeller insisted his name not appear on the campus. Over the years his gifts grew. A farewell gift of $10 million in 1910 brought his total contributions to about $35 million between 1892 and 1910. He later called the university the best investment he ever made.

The land for the main campus came from Marshall Field, owner of the Marshall Field and Company department store. He donated the original tract that holds the main quadrangles. Field was the largest single landholder and merchant in the city, and his gift placed the new university in Hyde Park on the South Side, near the lakefront site that would soon host the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition.

William Rainey Harper became the first president. Born July 24, 1856, in New Concord, Ohio, he was a child prodigy who earned a Yale doctorate in Semitic languages at nineteen and built a reputation as a Hebraist. Rockefeller chose the thirty-five-year-old Harper to organize the university. The Board of Trustees elected him president on September 18, 1890, and he took office on July 1, 1891.

Harper built an ambitious research university from the start. The first classes met on October 1, 1892, with an enrollment of 594 men and women and a faculty of about 120, including eight former college presidents Harper had recruited. The school was coeducational from its opening, unusual for the era.

Chicago architect Henry Ives Cobb laid out the campus plan and designed many of its early buildings in English Gothic Revival style, modeled on Oxford and Cambridge. The plan used interlocking quadrangles of gray limestone with corbels, crenellations, gargoyles, and grotesques. Cobb Lecture Hall was the first building completed and was ready for the October 1892 opening.

The Gothic quadrangles, the Field land gift, and Rockefeller's steady money turned a few South Side blocks into an anchor institution. The university drew faculty, students, housing, and commerce to Hyde Park. Its presence shaped the neighborhood's development for the next century, including later patterns of land control and displacement that the university itself would help drive.

narrationBeats: In the summer of 1893, Jackson Park held the World's Columbian Exposition, a world's fair built to mark 400 years since Columbus reached the Americas. The grounds covered more than 600 acres on the South Side lakefront, in and around what is now Hyde Park and Woodlawn.

Daniel Burnham ran the construction as Director of Works. The fair was dedicated on October 21, 1892, but it did not open to the public until May 1, 1893. It closed on October 30, 1893. Crews had broken ground in 1891, and at peak more than 40,000 workers were on site.

Frederick Law Olmsted, who had co-designed New York's Central Park decades earlier, designed the fairgrounds. He turned a marshy stretch of lakefront into lagoons and left a wooded island at the center. Olmsted and his firm placed the buildings and shaped the water and plantings that softened the formal architecture.

The core of the fair was the Court of Honor, a ring of huge neoclassical exhibit halls finished in white staff, a plaster and fiber mix. Lit at night by electricity, the gleaming buildings gave the fair its nickname, the White City. Most of the buildings were temporary and were never meant to last.

The Midway Plaisance, the mile-long strip connecting Jackson Park to Washington Park, held the amusement zone. There George Washington Gale Ferris Jr. built the first Ferris Wheel, an answer to the Eiffel Tower of the 1889 Paris fair. The wheel carried riders high above the Midway and helped draw crowds.

Attendance was enormous for its time. Sources put total attendance at roughly 27 million, with about 21.5 million paid admissions over the six months. On Chicago Day, October 9, 1893, paid admissions reached about 716,881, the largest single-day crowd at any world's fair to that point. October 9 was the anniversary of the start of the Great Chicago Fire of 1871.

Most of the White City did not survive. Fires and demolition cleared the temporary halls within a few years. The major lasting structure in Jackson Park is the former Palace of Fine Arts. Because foreign nations would not lend art for a non-fireproof building, it was built with a brick substructure, which is why it outlasted the rest.

The Palace of Fine Arts later housed the Field Columbian Museum, the start of what became the Field Museum, until that collection moved downtown in the 1920s. The building was rebuilt in permanent limestone between 1928 and 1933 and reopened as the Museum of Science and Industry, funded in part by Sears president Julius Rosenwald.

Olmsted's Wooded Island still sits in the lagoon at the heart of Jackson Park. The park itself remains an Olmsted landscape, and the fair shaped how Hyde Park and the surrounding South Side developed in the decades that followed.

verifiedBeats: In the summer of 1893, Jackson Park held the World's Columbian Exposition, a world's fair built to mark 400 years since Columbus reached the Americas. The grounds covered more than 600 acres on the South Side lakefront, in and around what is now Hyde Park and Woodlawn.

Daniel Burnham ran the construction as Director of Works. The fair was dedicated on October 21, 1892, but it did not open to the public until May 1, 1893. It closed on October 30, 1893. Crews had begun construction in January 1891, and at the height of the work more than 40,000 laborers were on site.

Frederick Law Olmsted, who had co-designed New York's Central Park decades earlier, designed the fairgrounds. He turned a marshy stretch of lakefront into lagoons and left a wooded island at the center. Olmsted and his firm placed the buildings and shaped the water and plantings that softened the formal architecture.

The core of the fair was the Court of Honor, a ring of huge neoclassical exhibit halls finished in white staff, a mix of plaster, cement, and jute fiber. Lit at night by electricity, the gleaming buildings gave the fair its nickname, the White City. Most of the buildings were temporary and were never meant to last.

The Midway Plaisance, the mile-long strip connecting Jackson Park to Washington Park, held the amusement zone. There George Washington Gale Ferris Jr. built the first Ferris Wheel, an answer to the Eiffel Tower of the 1889 Paris fair. The wheel carried riders high above the Midway and helped draw crowds.

Attendance was enormous for its time. Sources put total attendance at roughly 27 million, with about 21.5 million paid admissions over the six months. On Chicago Day, October 9, 1893, attendance reached about 751,000, a record outdoor crowd to that point. October 9 was the anniversary of the start of the Great Chicago Fire of 1871.

Most of the White City did not survive. Fires and demolition cleared the temporary halls within a few years. The major lasting structure in Jackson Park is the former Palace of Fine Arts. Because it held millions of dollars of art, it was built with a brick substructure to make it fireproof, which is why it outlasted the rest.

The Palace of Fine Arts later housed the Field Columbian Museum, the start of what became the Field Museum, until that collection moved to a new building near Grant Park in 1920. The old building was recast in limestone and reopened in 1933 as the Museum of Science and Industry, funded largely by Sears president Julius Rosenwald.

Olmsted's Wooded Island still sits in the lagoon at the heart of Jackson Park. The park itself remains an Olmsted landscape, and the fair shaped how Hyde Park and the surrounding South Side developed in the decades that followed.

script.voiceover: For six months in 1893, Jackson Park was not a park. It was a fair. The World's Columbian Exposition opened that May, built to mark four hundred years since Columbus reached the Americas. Daniel Burnham ran the construction. Frederick Law Olmsted turned the marshy lakefront into lagoons. At the center stood the Court of Honor, white plaster halls lit at night by electricity. People called it the White City. It was beautiful, and it was an argument. The fair staged the world as a ladder, with white northern Europe on top. Past the White City ran the Midway, where the fair set other peoples on display as a descending scale of civilization, a spectacle it dressed up as science. About twenty-seven million people came. Almost none of it was built to last. To move the crowds, the Illinois Central lifted its tracks onto an embankment above the streets. That wall of earth split the neighborhood in two, and the blocks toward the lake became a place apart, Hyde Park East. The fair made this lakefront valuable ground. The fight over who it belonged to was just ahead.

narrationBeats: The Great Migration reshaped Chicago. Black population in the city grew from about 40,000 in 1910 to 234,000 by 1930 and roughly 278,000 by 1940, as people left the South for jobs in meatpacking and manufacturing reached by the Illinois Central Railroad.

Most Black newcomers were confined to a narrow corridor on the South Side known as the Black Belt, kept there by violence, real estate practice, and the legal device of the racially restrictive covenant.

A restrictive covenant was a clause written into a property deed. It barred the owner from selling or renting to Black residents (the typical wording barred occupancy by any person of the Negro race). Neighbors signed in blocs so the rules covered whole streets.

Hyde Park and Kenwood, the neighborhoods around the University of Chicago, used these covenants heavily. A first wave was recorded in 1928 and 1929 across the belt of communities ringing the Black Belt, namely Kenwood, Oakland, Hyde Park, Woodlawn, South Shore, Greater Grand Crossing, Englewood, and West Englewood.

The University of Chicago supported this system. Historians including Arnold Hirsch and LaDale Winling document that the university worked through neighborhood property owners associations to keep the area around campus white, and the university funded the legal defense of restrictive covenants.

Local property owners groups enforced the covenants directly. The Hyde Park-Kenwood Property Owners Association backed covenants and filed suits to remove Black families who moved into covered housing.

Black Chicagoans fought the covenants in court. In Hansberry v. Lee, decided by the U.S. Supreme Court on November 12, 1940, Carl Hansberry challenged a covenant in the Washington Park subdivision of Woodlawn. The Court ruled in his favor on procedural grounds (the earlier class action did not bind him), but it did not strike covenants down. Carl Hansberry's daughter Lorraine later drew on the family's experience for the play A Raisin in the Sun.

The decisive case came from St. Louis, not Chicago. In Shelley v. Kraemer, decided May 3, 1948, the Supreme Court held that courts could not enforce racially restrictive covenants because judicial enforcement counted as state action barred by the Fourteenth Amendment. Chief Justice Fred Vinson wrote for a unanimous Court (6 to 0, with three justices recused).
Shelley did not make the covenants disappear from deeds. It made them legally unenforceable, so a court could no longer evict a Black family for violating one.

After 1948, Black families began moving into Hyde Park and Kenwood. The transition was rapid in parts of Kenwood. This change set the stage for the University of Chicago sponsored urban renewal of the 1950s and 1960s, which reshaped the neighborhood and is the subject of the next chapter.

script.voiceover: It started with a club. In 1908, white homeowners formed the Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club, three hundred and fifty strong, with a single aim, to remove every Black resident and worker from the neighborhood. They pledged to fire their Black servants, to boycott any agent who sold to a Black family, and to buy out the Black households who had lived here for years. One of them, Fannie Barrier Williams, a longtime resident, refused to leave. When pressure was not enough, they turned to the deed. A racially restrictive covenant was a line written into the title, barring sale or rent to anyone who was not white. Neighbors signed in blocs, so a single clause could seal a whole block. And the University of Chicago was not a bystander. Between 1933 and 1947 it spent more than eighty-three thousand dollars defending the covenants around its campus. Black Chicago kept growing the whole time, from about forty thousand people in 1910 to two hundred seventy-eight thousand by 1940. Most were pressed into a narrow corridor called the Black Belt, a few blocks wide and miles long. Inside it families paid more for less, carved into kitchenette apartments, because the color line left them nowhere else to go.

script.voiceover: The belief that a Black family lowered the value of a block was not only prejudice. It was given the authority of science, right here. A University of Chicago economist named Homer Hoyt ranked races and nationalities by their supposed effect on land values. Then he carried that logic to Washington, as the federal government's chief land economist, where it was drawn onto maps. Block by block, neighborhoods with Black residents were outlined and marked hazardous, then cut off from loans. The country would come to call it redlining, and it spread to nearly every major city in America. An idea built in a Hyde Park classroom helped wall off the whole country. Not until 1948 did the Supreme Court take the covenants' force away, in Shelley versus Kraemer. The clauses stayed in the deeds. The courts just could not enforce them anymore.

narrationBeats: In March 1952 an attempted assault on a University of Chicago graduate student near campus brought long-simmering fears about crime to a head. The university convened a mass meeting, and out of it came a new organization. The South East Chicago Commission was established in May 1952 to coordinate police protection, building-code enforcement, and a plan to redevelop the neighborhood the university called home.

University Chancellor Lawrence A. Kimpton chaired the commission. Its executive director was Julian H. Levi, a corporate lawyer who ran the program from 1952 until 1980. Levi was the day-to-day engine of renewal in Hyde Park-Kenwood. He worked the city, the state legislature, and Congress to build the legal tools that clearance required.

The university was open about what it was doing and why. By its own accounting it committed roughly 29 million dollars of its own money to buy, control, and rebuild the surrounding blocks. Levi and Kimpton treated the survival of the university as bound up with controlling who lived nearby and what condition the buildings were in.

The timing matters. After the Supreme Court made racially restrictive covenants unenforceable in 1948, Black families began moving into Hyde Park and Kenwood in large numbers through the early 1950s. The renewal program was designed in that context. Arnold Hirsch, in Making the Second Ghetto, argues the program was built specifically to manage racial succession rather than simply to fix old buildings.

Demolition did not wait for a finished plan. The first building in the Hyde Park A project came down on May 10, 1955. Federal funding for the larger effort followed in the mid-1950s. Smaller projects, Hyde Park A and B, moved first while planners drafted the comprehensive program.

The big plan, the Hyde Park-Kenwood Urban Renewal Plan, was not formally approved by the Chicago City Council until November 7, 1958. Kimpton testified before the council in support of it. The plan covered roughly 856 acres, called for demolishing about 638 buildings, and displaced about 4,000 families.

Levi helped write the federal rules he then used. Section 112 of the Housing Act, enacted in 1959, let a university count its own spending near campus as the local matching share of a federal urban renewal grant, and credited institutional expansion as a public purpose. It nationalized a tool forged in Hyde Park. After it passed, the university turned next toward Woodlawn.

The human cost fell unevenly by race. Records from the Hyde Park A and B projects show that about 46 percent of displaced white families found new homes within Hyde Park-Kenwood, compared with only about 17 percent of displaced Black families. The South West Hyde Park area cleared by a university-owned development corporation was roughly 80 percent Black at the time of acquisition.

Across the 1960s the neighborhood lost population. Hyde Park-Kenwood fell from about 71,000 residents before renewal to about 46,000 by 1970, a drop of nearly 28 percent. The replacement housing was newer and more expensive, and many of the low-income Black residents whose homes were demolished could not afford to return.

The defenders called it renewal, the country's first big neighborhood to ask for planned redevelopment, and they pointed to a stable integrated community that survived. Critics used a sharper phrase. James Baldwin called this kind of program Negro removal. Both descriptions point at the same record. The neighborhood was preserved, and a large share of its poorest Black residents were moved out to do it.

narrationBeats: Open standing in the present. The Obama Presidential Center is finished. It opened to the public on June 19, 2026, Juneteenth, after a dedication ceremony the day before. The host can stand with the museum tower in frame, a 225 foot stone shaft rising over Jackson Park where the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition once stood.

State the basic facts of the building plainly. Designed by Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects, the campus cost roughly 850 million dollars, making it by far the most expensive presidential library project in American history. It holds a museum, a branch of the Chicago Public Library, conference and community space, an athletic facility, and the offices of the Obama Foundation, all set in landscaped park.

Tell the long road. The site was chosen in 2016. Construction did not actually begin until August 2021, and the Obamas, Governor J.B. Pritzker, and Mayor Lori Lightfoot held the groundbreaking on September 28, 2021. The delay came from a federal environmental and historic preservation review, since Jackson Park was laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and sits on the National Register of Historic Places.

Name the fight over the park itself. A group called Protect Our Parks sued repeatedly to stop construction, arguing that putting a private institution's building on Olmsted parkland broke the public trust and that the federal review of alternatives was flawed. The federal review itself acknowledged the Center would alter the historic park's design integrity. Courts dismissed the suits and construction went forward. This is the preservation versus institutions tension made concrete.

Pivot to the people who live around it. Years before the building rose, neighborhood organizers saw the displacement coming. The Obama CBA Coalition, led by groups like KOCO, STOP, and BYP100, formed in 2016 to demand a community benefits agreement so that longtime Black residents of Woodlawn and South Shore would not be priced out by the investment the Center attracted.

Give the housing numbers, which are the heart of the close. In September 2020 the City Council passed the Woodlawn Housing Preservation Ordinance after a roughly five year campaign. It set aside city owned vacant lots for affordable units and funded homebuyer help. But by 2026 the protections were widely judged too weak. Home prices on the east side of Woodlawn, closest to the Center, had doubled since 2019. In the city's Jackson Park housing pilot area, median rents rose 43 percent and home values 130 percent since 2015, and by 2024 less than a third of the housing stock was affordable, half the share of fifteen years earlier.

Show the second front, the university. The University of Chicago, the area's dominant institution, kept expanding south across the Midway into Woodlawn through the 2020s with projects like the Woodlawn Residential Commons for roughly 1,200 students. The university now owns or invests in hundreds of properties across Hyde Park and nearby neighborhoods. The host should connect this directly to the opening thesis, because the same institutional pattern that produced 1950s and 60s urban renewal, which displaced thousands of families, is still shaping who can afford to stay.

Close on the unresolved tension. Hyde Park today is a neighborhood of a world class university, a new presidential center, an Olmsted lakefront, and residents organizing block by block to not be pushed out by the very investment that makes the place desirable. The host names the throughline of the whole tour. Powerful institutions reshape this ground, the public good they promise is real, and the cost of that reshaping has fallen, again and again, on the people with the least power to absorb it. End looking at the lakefront, the question left open rather than answered.

The 1950s and 60s Hyde Park-Kenwood urban renewal program, backed by the University, displaced roughly 4,000 families.

verifiedFacts: The Obama Presidential Center opened to the public on June 19, 2026 (Juneteenth), after a dedication ceremony held June 18, 2026. Grand Opening Weekend events followed June 20 to 21. (Confirmed: Obama Foundation, Wikipedia, CBS News, Newsweek.)

Construction began in August 2021, and the groundbreaking ceremony with the Obamas, Gov. J.B. Pritzker, and former Mayor Lori Lightfoot was held September 28, 2021. The delay followed a multi-year federal review that concluded in 2021. (Confirmed: Obama Foundation press release, PBS, Wikipedia.)

The Center was designed by Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects, cost about $850 million (up from a roughly $350 million initial projection), and its museum tower stands about 225 feet (69 m) tall. The campus is 19.3 acres. (Confirmed: CNN, Dezeen, TWBTA, Newsweek.)

The Center is widely described as the most expensive presidential center in U.S. history. Note it is privately operated and is not a traditional NARA-run presidential library, so 'center' rather than 'library' is the precise framing. (Confirmed: ThePrint, CoStar, CNN.)

Jackson Park was laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux (1871), hosted the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972. (Confirmed: TCLF, City of Chicago.)

The project triggered a federal Section 106 historic-preservation review under the 1966 National Historic Preservation Act. A draft Assessment of Effects concluded the Center as planned would significantly diminish the integrity of the Olmsted-designed landscape. (Confirmed: TCLF, City of Chicago, WTTW.)

Protect Our Parks filed repeated lawsuits arguing the Center violated the public-trust doctrine by placing a private institution on Jackson Park parkland leased for 99 years at $10. The litigation was ultimately unsuccessful and construction proceeded, though the path was not a single clean dismissal. The Seventh Circuit at one point remanded the case, finding some claims should have been dismissed; later suits were tossed by the district court. (Confirmed: CBS Chicago, HP Herald, Courthouse News, U.S. Supreme Court docket.)

The Obama CBA Coalition formed in 2016 (after the 2015-2016 site selection) and included KOCO, STOP, and BYP100. The Woodlawn Housing Preservation Ordinance passed City Council unanimously on September 9, 2020. It applied to 52 city-owned vacant lots (requiring 30 percent affordable units for very-low-income households) and funded a loan fund and the Renew Woodlawn program. (Confirmed: Block Club Chicago, Woods Fund, City of Chicago, STOP.)

By 2026 the protections were widely judged too weak. Single-family home prices in East Woodlawn, nearest the Center, doubled from 2019 to a 2025 median of about $440,000 (Institute for Housing Studies). In the city's Jackson Park Housing Pilot area, median rents rose 43 percent and home values 130 percent since 2015 (mayor's office), and by 2024 less than a third of the housing stock was affordable, half the share of 15 years earlier. (Confirmed: Illinois Answers Project, May 7, 2026; Block Club Chicago.)

The University of Chicago opened the Woodlawn Residential Commons in 2020, housing about 1,200 to 1,300 students, and per a 2025 Chicago Maroon data project owns or invests in over 250 properties (300-plus including past holdings) across Hyde Park and nearby neighborhoods. (Confirmed: Chicago Maroon, UChicago Facilities.)

The 1950s-60s Hyde Park-Kenwood urban renewal program, sponsored by the University of Chicago, displaced roughly 4,000 families. (Confirmed: Chicago Magazine; consistent with Hirsch and Winling. A separate figure of 'over 15,000 residents' also circulates; the ~4,000 family count is the defensible one to cite.)

script.voiceover: The Obama Presidential Center opened on June 19, 2026. Juneteenth. The museum tower runs about two hundred twenty-five feet over Jackson Park. Olmsted and Vaux laid out this park in 1871, and it's the same ground that held the 1893 World's Fair. The campus cost about eight hundred fifty million dollars. No presidential center has ever cost more. Getting it built took years. The site was picked in 2016. A group called Protect Our Parks sued over and over to stop it. Every suit failed. Construction started in 2021. And while the Center went up, Woodlawn got more expensive. On the blocks closest to it, home prices doubled after 2019. By 2024, less than a third of the housing nearby was still affordable. The pattern that began with the covenants never really broke. When Black families finally bought here, and across the South and West Sides, many bought on contract, at markups that stripped an estimated three to four billion dollars from Black Chicago. Money that should have become wealth, handed down, simply vanished. You can still measure the hole it left. Today the median white family in America holds about two hundred eighty-five thousand dollars. The median Black family holds about forty-five thousand. A gap of more than six to one. It is a pattern the neighborhood has run before. An institution arrives, the ground around it gains value, and the people already there are left to wonder if the new Hyde Park has room for them. A hundred and seventy years after Paul Cornell bought these blocks, the question underneath it all, who this ground is for, still is not settled.

script.hostScript: I'm standing in Jackson Park, and behind me is the Obama Presidential Center. People waited more than a decade for this to become reality, and for many, it's a major investment in the South Side. But there's another side of the story that didn't make it into the ribbon-cutting. As the Center was being built, Woodlawn, the neighborhood that worked for years to bring it here, became far more expensive. On the blocks closest to the project, home prices doubled. So I keep coming back to one question. When investment transforms a neighborhood, who gets to stay and be part of what they helped create?
